slides: Open by treating Chapter 0 as a working contract for the rest of Geometry I. The point is not to memorize a glossary, but to notice which symbols will later carry geometry: sets become spaces, maps become motions, algebra records composition, and metrics give numerical tests.

Use the pipeline as the lecture promise. A notation mark is never just ink; it selects an object, a model, and a check. Emphasize that the notebook rebuilds this habit visually, so students can inspect the same convention as a diagram or certificate.

Spend a minute separating three questions students often compress. What is the point-level rule, what subset is being transported, and which codomain is being used? Preimages are especially important because topology and measure are usually pulled back through maps rather than pushed forward.

Connect this slide to Chapter 1, where actions become central. The background convention is already doing real work: composition order, identity elements, inverses, kernels, and images all become ways to check whether a symbolic calculation still describes the intended geometric motion.

Pause on the infimum in the set distance formula. It explains why a picture of nearest approach is only a guide until the space and sets are specified. For compact sets in Euclidean space the infimum is attained, but the background language is written broadly enough for later settings.

Frame compactness as the move from infinite local information to finite usable data. This prepares students for existence arguments later in the course: a minimizing sequence, a covering argument, or a continuity claim becomes reliable only after the topology says which limits are allowed.

Treat this as a preview rather than a full analysis lecture. Measure gives later geometry a way to average, integrate, and compare sizes robustly. Hyperbolic functions enter because some geometric models have an identity with a minus sign, so the familiar trigonometric pattern changes its metric meaning.

Close with the checklist as a reusable preflight routine. Before students solve a later problem, they can identify the space, map, metric, topology, and invariant. That habit prevents many errors because it forces every symbolic step to remain attached to a geometric object.
